title: JIT Caching in CuTe DSL
critical_patterns: First kernel run compiles and caches
Subsequent runs use cache for speedup
Cache key depends on function source, parameter types, and compilation options
Precompile kernels with cute.compile() for faster execution later
Clear cache manually or set automatic cleanup policies
constraints: Cache key is affected by function source code, parameter types, constexpr values, compilation options, and target architecture
Cache does not persist across CuTe DSL updates if format changes
Different GPUs with different architectures require separate caches
Cache should not be shared across users
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL employs a JIT caching mechanism to store compiled GPU kernels, significantly reducing execution time on subsequent runs by avoiding recompilation. The cache is stored in the user's home directory under ~/.cache/cutlass/ and persists across Python sessions and system reboots, but may be invalidated by updates to the CuTe DSL. Cache keys are generated based on the function's source code, parameter types, constexpr values, compilation options, and target architecture, but not by runtime parameter values or tensor data. Developers can precompile kernels using cute.compile() to warm up the cache and ensure fast execution in production. Cache management includes clearing the cache manually or setting environment variables for automatic cleanup. During development, caching can be disabled to ensure recompilation for debugging purposes. Best practices involve warming the cache at application startup, monitoring cache size, and clearing the cache after DSL updates. Performance gains from caching are substantial, with cached calls executing in milliseconds compared to seconds for the initial compilation. Developers should avoid disabling the cache in production and ensure that cache directories are not included in version control.
